title: Ch3: Principles of Reliable Data Transfer (rdt1.0 to rdt3.0)

questions.q: In the rdt interface model, which function does the application (the upper layer) call to hand data to the sender side of the reliable data transfer protocol?
choices: rdt_send()
udt_send()
rdt_rcv()
deliver_data()
questions.explain: rdt_send() is called from above (for example by the app) and is passed the data to deliver to the receiver's upper layer. udt_send() is what rdt itself calls to put a packet on the unreliable channel.

questions.q: Which function does the rdt implementation call to transfer a packet over the unreliable channel?
choices: rdt_send()
udt_send()
rdt_rcv()
deliver_data()
questions.explain: udt_send() ('unreliable data transfer' send) is called by rdt to send a packet over the unreliable channel. It is used in both directions: for data packets from the sender and for ACK/NAK packets from the receiver.

questions.q: Which sequence of calls correctly traces one chunk of data from the sending application to the receiving application?
choices: rdt_send() -> udt_send() -> rdt_rcv() -> deliver_data()
udt_send() -> rdt_send() -> deliver_data() -> rdt_rcv()
rdt_send() -> rdt_rcv() -> udt_send() -> deliver_data()
deliver_data() -> udt_send() -> rdt_rcv() -> rdt_send()
questions.explain: The app calls rdt_send(data). The sender side builds a packet and calls udt_send(). When the packet arrives on the receiver side of the channel, rdt_rcv() is invoked, and the receiver then calls deliver_data() to pass the data up.

questions.q: In the rdt interface diagram, how does a 'packet' on the channel differ from the 'data' the application hands down?
choices: The sender-side rdt adds a header to the data, so a packet is header + data
A packet is the data with its checksum removed
A packet is identical to the data; the names refer to the same bytes
A packet holds only control information; the data travels separately
questions.explain: The transport layer adds a header to the application data to form a packet (segment). The receiver side processes the header and passes only the data up through deliver_data().

questions.q: Because rdt only considers unidirectional data transfer, nothing ever travels from the receiver side back to the sender side over the channel.
questions.explain: Data flows one way only, but control information (ACKs, NAKs) flows in both directions. The communication between the two protocol sides over the unreliable channel is bidirectional.

questions.q: What most strongly determines how complex the sender and receiver sides of a reliable data transfer protocol must be?
choices: The size of each application message
How fast the sending application produces data
The characteristics of the underlying unreliable channel: whether it can lose, corrupt, or reorder data
How many application processes run on each host
questions.explain: Protocol complexity depends strongly on what the unreliable channel can do. With a perfect channel (rdt1.0) the protocol is trivial. Bit errors need checksums, ACK/NAKs, retransmission and sequence numbers. Loss also needs timers.

questions.q: The slides draw a curtain between the sender and receiver sides of the protocol. What point does this make?
choices: Neither side knows the other's state (for example, whether a message was received) unless that is communicated through a message
The receiver cannot read the header fields the sender adds
The channel hides packet contents by encrypting them
The sender can observe the receiver's state directly, but not the other way around
questions.explain: Each side can learn about the other only through messages sent over the channel. For example, the sender learns that a packet arrived correctly only when an ACK comes back. That is why a protocol is needed.

questions.q: In an FSM specification of a protocol, what does being in a particular 'state' mean?
choices: The next state is uniquely determined by the next event
The protocol has finished sending all of its data
No events can occur until a timer expires
The sender and receiver must be in matching states
questions.explain: When the machine is in a given state, the next state is uniquely determined by the next event. Transitions are triggered by events and may perform actions.

questions.q: An FSM transition is labeled with text above a horizontal line and text below it. What goes where?
choices: Above: the event that causes the transition. Below: the actions taken on the transition
Above: the actions taken. Below: the event that causes the transition
Above: the current state. Below: the next state
Above: the sender's actions. Below: the receiver's actions
questions.explain: Example: rdt_send(data) (the event) above the line, and packet = make_pkt(data); udt_send(packet) (the actions) below it.

questions.q: Which Greek letter, written in the action position of an rdt FSM transition, means that no action is taken?
questions.explain: Λ (lambda) means no action. For example, when the rdt2.0 sender in 'Wait for ACK or NAK' receives an ACK, it returns to 'Wait for call from above' with Λ.

questions.q: Which assumptions does rdt1.0 make about the underlying channel?
choices: No bit errors
No loss of packets
Bits may be flipped, but packets are never lost
Packets may be lost, but are never corrupted
questions.explain: rdt1.0 is reliable transfer over a perfectly reliable channel: no bit errors and no packet loss. Because of that, the sender just sends and the receiver just reads.

questions.q: What does the rdt1.0 receiver do when the event rdt_rcv(packet) occurs?
choices: extract(packet, data), then deliver_data(data)
Verify the checksum, then send an ACK
Send a NAK if the packet is corrupted
Start a timer and wait to see whether a duplicate arrives
questions.explain: The channel is perfect, so the receiver has a single state ('Wait for call from below'). It extracts the data and delivers it up. It sends no feedback at all.

questions.q: How many states does the rdt1.0 sender FSM have?
questions.explain: One state, 'Wait for call from above'. On rdt_send(data) it does make_pkt and udt_send and stays in that state. The rdt1.0 receiver also has a single state, 'Wait for call from below'.

questions.q: In the light-bulb example used to introduce FSMs, which choice correctly identifies the states and the events?
choices: States: on and off. Events: the switch being turned on or off
States: switch turned on and switch turned off. Events: light emitted and light stopped
State: emitting light. Events: on and off
One state (the bulb) and two actions (on and off)
questions.explain: The bulb is in the on state or the off state. Flipping the switch is the event that causes a transition between them, and emitting or stopping light is the resulting action. A complete spec also says what happens if 'on' is pressed while the bulb is already on.

questions.q: rdt2.0 assumes the channel may flip bits in a packet. What does it use to detect those bit errors?
questions.explain: A checksum (for example the Internet checksum) is included in each packet, via make_pkt(data, checksum), so the receiver can detect corruption.

questions.q: Which mechanisms does rdt2.0 use to deal with bit errors?
choices: A checksum for error detection
Acknowledgements (ACKs)
Negative acknowledgements (NAKs)
Retransmission when a NAK is received
A sequence number on each packet
A countdown timer
questions.explain: rdt2.0 uses a checksum, ACKs (packet received OK), NAKs (packet had errors), and retransmission on NAK. Sequence numbers first appear in rdt2.1, and timers in rdt3.0.

questions.q: rdt2.0 is described as a 'stop-and-wait' protocol. What does that mean?
choices: The sender sends one packet, then waits for the receiver's response before going on
The receiver stops accepting packets until the application reads the earlier ones
The sender stops transmitting whenever a timer expires
The channel stops delivering packets once it detects an error
questions.explain: Stop-and-wait means the sender sends one packet, then waits for the receiver's response (ACK or NAK) before it accepts more data from above.

questions.q: The rdt2.0 sender is in 'Wait for ACK or NAK' and receives a NAK. What does it do?
choices: Retransmits the same packet (udt_send(sndpkt)) and stays in 'Wait for ACK or NAK'
Drops the packet and returns to 'Wait for call from above'
Builds a new packet from the next chunk of application data
Sends a NAK back to the receiver
questions.explain: On rdt_rcv(rcvpkt) && isNAK(rcvpkt), the sender resends the stored sndpkt and keeps waiting. Only an ACK returns it to 'Wait for call from above'.

questions.q: While in 'Wait for ACK or NAK', the rdt2.0 sender can accept new data from the application through rdt_send().
questions.explain: rdt_send() is handled only in 'Wait for call from above'. While waiting for an ACK or NAK the sender cannot take new data. This is the stop-and-wait behavior.

questions.q: The rdt2.0 receiver gets a packet and the checksum shows it is corrupted. What does it do?
choices: Sends a NAK and does not deliver the data
Delivers the data and sends a NAK
Discards the packet silently and sends nothing
Sends an ACK so the sender will move on to the next packet
questions.explain: On rdt_rcv(rcvpkt) && corrupt(rcvpkt), the receiver does udt_send(NAK). Only an uncorrupted packet is extracted, delivered with deliver_data(), and answered with an ACK.

questions.q: In rdt2.0, the first transmission of a data packet is corrupted and the retransmission arrives intact (ACKs and NAKs are not corrupted). Counting both data packets and ACK/NAK packets, how many packets cross the channel before the sender is back in 'Wait for call from above'?
questions.explain: Data packet (corrupted), then NAK, then the retransmitted data packet (OK), then ACK. That is 4 packets in total.

questions.q: In a conversation, a listener says 'I don't understand what you said,' and the speaker repeats the sentence. Which pair of rdt mechanisms does this correspond to?
choices: A negative acknowledgement followed by a retransmission
An acknowledgement followed by a sequence number
A checksum followed by a timeout
A duplicate ACK followed by a timer restart
questions.explain: Humans recover from errors with ACKs ('yes, I got it'), NAKs ('I didn't understand'), and retransmission (repeating the message). rdt2.0 is built on the same mechanisms.

questions.q: What is rdt2.0's 'fatal flaw'?
choices: If an ACK or NAK is corrupted, the sender doesn't know what happened at the receiver
It cannot detect bit errors in data packets
It delivers packets out of order because it sends several at once
It sends so many NAKs that it wastes bandwidth
questions.explain: rdt2.0 does not handle a garbled ACK or NAK. The sender can't tell whether the receiver got the packet, and it can't just retransmit, because that might create a duplicate.

questions.q: Suppose an rdt2.0-style sender simply retransmitted whenever an ACK or NAK arrived garbled, with nothing else added. What could go wrong?
choices: If the garbled reply was really an ACK, the receiver would get a copy of data it already has and deliver it as new data
The receiver would answer every retransmission with a NAK, forever
The checksum of the retransmitted packet would be computed incorrectly
The sender would deadlock waiting for a timeout that never comes
questions.explain: The receiver has no way to tell a retransmission from new data, so the old data would be passed to the application twice. Sequence numbers fix this.

questions.q: How does rdt2.1 handle a corrupted ACK or NAK without causing duplicate delivery?
choices: The sender retransmits the current packet if the ACK/NAK is corrupted
The sender adds a sequence number to each packet
The receiver discards duplicate packets instead of delivering them up
The receiver delivers duplicates and leaves it to the application to discard them
The sender waits for a timeout before retransmitting
questions.explain: Retransmit on a garbled ACK/NAK, number each packet, and have the receiver drop duplicates (not deliver them up). rdt2.1 has no timer; timers come in rdt3.0.

questions.q: Why are just two sequence numbers (0 and 1) enough for rdt2.1?
choices: With stop-and-wait only one packet is outstanding, so the receiver only has to tell the next new packet apart from a retransmission of the previous one
The channel never reorders more than two packets
Sequence numbers are reused only after a timeout guarantees that old packets are gone
The checksum already identifies each packet uniquely, so the bit only marks ACK versus NAK
questions.explain: The sender doesn't send a new packet until the current one is acknowledged. Any arriving packet is therefore either the expected new one or a resend of the last one, and a 1-bit sequence number tells them apart.

questions.q: How many states does the rdt2.1 sender FSM have?
questions.explain: Four: 'Wait for call 0 from above', 'Wait for ACK or NAK 0', 'Wait for call 1 from above', and 'Wait for ACK or NAK 1'. That is twice rdt2.0's two states, because the state must remember whether the current packet has sequence number 0 or 1.

questions.q: The rdt2.1 receiver is in 'Wait for 1 from below' and receives an uncorrupted packet with sequence number 0. What does it do?
choices: Sends an ACK, does not deliver the data, and stays in 'Wait for 1 from below'
Sends a NAK so the sender will transmit packet 1
Delivers the data and moves to 'Wait for 0 from below'
Delivers the data again and sends an ACK
questions.explain: Packet 0 is a duplicate of data already delivered, so the sender evidently didn't get a good ACK for it. The receiver sends an ACK (not a NAK) so the sender can move on, and it does not deliver the data again.

questions.q: The rdt2.1 sender is in 'Wait for ACK or NAK 1' and receives a corrupted packet. What does it do?
choices: Retransmits the packet with sequence number 1 and stays in the same state
Moves to 'Wait for call 0 from above'
Sends a NAK to the receiver
Sends a new packet with sequence number 0
questions.explain: On rdt_rcv(rcvpkt) && (corrupt(rcvpkt) || isNAK(rcvpkt)), the sender resends sndpkt, which is the seq-1 packet, and keeps waiting.

questions.q: In rdt2.1, the receiver can tell whether its last ACK or NAK was received correctly by the sender.
questions.explain: The receiver cannot know whether its last ACK/NAK arrived OK. It just responds to whatever arrives: NAK a corrupted packet, ACK a duplicate, and deliver and ACK the expected packet.

questions.q: rdt2.1: pkt0 arrives intact, the receiver delivers it and sends an ACK, but the ACK is corrupted on the way back. What happens next?
choices: The sender retransmits pkt0. The receiver, now waiting for 1, sees a duplicate, doesn't deliver it, and sends an ACK
The sender assumes success and sends pkt1
The sender retransmits pkt0, and the receiver delivers it a second time and sends an ACK
The sender retransmits pkt0, and the receiver sends a NAK because it expected sequence number 1
questions.explain: A garbled ACK/NAK makes the sender resend the current packet. The sequence number lets the receiver recognize the duplicate, discard it, and ACK it, and that ACK lets the sender move to pkt1.

questions.q: How does rdt2.2 provide the same functionality as rdt2.1 without using NAKs?
choices: Instead of a NAK, the receiver sends an ACK for the last packet received OK, explicitly including that packet's sequence number
The receiver stays silent on errors and the sender relies on a timer
The sender transmits every packet twice
The receiver signals an error by sending an ACK with an inverted checksum
questions.explain: rdt2.2 uses ACKs only. Re-ACKing the last good packet tells the sender that the current packet was not received OK.

questions.q: The rdt2.2 sender is in 'Wait for ACK 0' and receives an uncorrupted ACK carrying sequence number 1. What does it do?
choices: Retransmits the current packet (sequence number 0)
Treats it as success and returns to wait for the next call from above
Ignores it and waits for a timeout
Sends a packet with sequence number 1
questions.explain: A duplicate ACK (ACK1 while waiting for ACK0) has the same effect as a NAK, so the sender retransmits the current packet. The rdt2.2 sender has no timer to wait on.

questions.q: In rdt2.2, the receiver must explicitly include the sequence number of the packet being ACKed.
questions.explain: Without NAKs, the sender can tell 'got the current packet' from 'still stuck on the previous one' only by the sequence number in the ACK, for example isACK(rcvpkt,0) versus isACK(rcvpkt,1).

questions.q: The rdt2.2 receiver is in 'Wait for 0 from below' (it has just accepted pkt1) and receives a corrupted packet. What does it send?
choices: ACK1 again: it re-sends its last ACK, for the last packet it received OK
A NAK
ACK0
Nothing
questions.explain: On corrupt(rcvpkt) || has_seq1(rcvpkt), the receiver calls udt_send(sndpkt), which still holds ACK1 from when it accepted pkt1. The sender sees a duplicate ACK and retransmits pkt0.

questions.q: rdt2.2 introduces a protocol mechanism that rdt2.1 does not have.
questions.explain: rdt2.2 adds no new mechanism. It uses the existing ones (ACKs with sequence numbers, checksums, retransmission) differently, so that it can drop NAKs.

questions.q: Which real transport protocol uses rdt2.2's NAK-free approach, relying on ACKs along with sequence numbers, checksums, and retransmissions?
questions.explain: TCP is NAK-free. A duplicate ACK signals that something after the acknowledged data was not received correctly.

questions.q: What new assumption about the underlying channel does rdt3.0 add?
choices: The channel can also lose packets, both data packets and ACKs
The channel can reorder packets arbitrarily
The channel can duplicate packets but never corrupt them
The channel is error-free but has variable delay
questions.explain: rdt3.0 keeps bit errors and adds packet loss. Checksums, sequence numbers, ACKs and retransmissions help, but they are not enough on their own.

questions.q: What mechanism does rdt3.0 add to cope with lost packets?
choices: A countdown timer: the sender retransmits if no ACK arrives within a 'reasonable' amount of time
NAKs from the receiver whenever it notices a packet has gone missing
Multi-bit sequence numbers instead of a single bit
A second checksum covering only the header
questions.explain: The sender waits a 'reasonable' time for an ACK and retransmits if none arrives. A countdown timer interrupts it when that time is up. The receiver can't send a NAK for a packet it never saw.

questions.q: If a packet or ACK is only delayed (not lost), the sender's timeout causes an unnecessary retransmission. What keeps this from causing duplicate data to be delivered?
choices: Sequence numbers let the receiver recognize the retransmission as a duplicate
The checksum marks the retransmitted packet as a duplicate
The timer is cancelled automatically when the delayed packet reaches the receiver
Nothing; rdt3.0 assumes packets are never delayed
questions.explain: The retransmission will be a duplicate, but sequence numbers already handle that. The receiver also has to put the sequence number of the packet being ACKed in its ACK.

questions.q: The rdt3.0 sender is in 'Wait for ACK0' and receives a corrupted packet or an ACK with sequence number 1. What does it do?
choices: Nothing (Λ). It keeps waiting, and the timeout will cause the retransmission if one is needed
Retransmits packet 0 immediately
Stops the timer and returns to 'Wait for call 0 from above'
Sends packet 1
questions.explain: In rdt3.0, rdt_rcv(rcvpkt) && (corrupt(rcvpkt) || isACK(rcvpkt,1)) has action Λ, and the timer handles recovery. This differs from rdt2.2, where a duplicate ACK triggers an immediate retransmission.

questions.q: Which events make the rdt3.0 sender call start_timer?
choices: Sending a new packet after rdt_send(data)
Retransmitting the packet after a timeout
Receiving a corrupted ACK
Receiving the ACK it was waiting for
questions.explain: Every udt_send(sndpkt) is followed by start_timer, both the first send and the resend on timeout. A corrupted or wrong ACK has action Λ, and the expected ACK leads to stop_timer.

questions.q: When does the rdt3.0 sender call stop_timer?
choices: When it receives an uncorrupted ACK with the expected sequence number
When it receives any ACK, even a corrupted one
Immediately after udt_send(sndpkt)
Only when the timeout fires
questions.explain: rdt_rcv(rcvpkt) && notcorrupt(rcvpkt) && isACK(rcvpkt,0) in 'Wait for ACK0' (or ACK 1 in 'Wait for ACK1') triggers stop_timer and the move to wait for the next call from above.

questions.q: If the rdt3.0 sender is in 'Wait for call 0 from above' and a packet arrives from the channel (for example a late, duplicate ACK), it takes no action.
questions.explain: Both 'Wait for call from above' states have a self-loop rdt_rcv(rcvpkt) with action Λ. Packets arriving then are ignored.

questions.q: In rdt3.0, the receiver detects that a packet was lost and notifies the sender.
questions.explain: The receiver never learns about a packet it didn't get. The sender detects loss, of the packet or of its ACK, when its countdown timer expires without the expected ACK, and then retransmits.

questions.q: rdt3.0: the sender sends pkt1 and it is lost in the channel. What happens?
choices: The sender's timer expires, it resends pkt1, and the receiver receives it and sends ack1
The receiver notices the gap and sends a NAK for pkt1
The receiver re-sends ack0, which makes the sender retransmit pkt1 immediately
The sender gives up on pkt1 and moves on to the next packet, pkt0
questions.explain: This is the packet-loss case. Nothing comes back, the timeout fires, pkt1 is resent and acknowledged with ack1, and the sender then continues with pkt0.

questions.q: rdt3.0: pkt1 arrives intact and the receiver sends ack1, but ack1 is lost. What happens next?
choices: The sender times out and resends pkt1. The receiver detects the duplicate, does not deliver it again, and sends ack1
The sender times out and moves on to send pkt0
The receiver times out and resends ack1 on its own
The sender times out and resends pkt1, and the receiver delivers it again and sends ack1
questions.explain: This is the ACK-loss case. To the sender, a lost ACK looks the same as a lost packet, so it retransmits after the timeout. The sequence number lets the receiver detect the duplicate and just re-ACK it.

questions.q: rdt3.0 premature timeout: ack1 is delayed (not lost), so the sender times out and resends pkt1. The delayed ack1 then arrives and the sender sends pkt0. Later, a second ack1 (the receiver's reply to the duplicate pkt1) arrives while the sender is waiting for ack0. What does the sender do with it?
choices: Ignores it
Retransmits pkt0
Retransmits pkt1
Stops the timer and waits for a call from above
questions.explain: In 'Wait for ACK0', an isACK(rcvpkt,1) has action Λ, so the extra ack1 is ignored. The receiver has meanwhile detected the duplicate pkt1 and not delivered it, so the transfer continues correctly.

questions.q: rdt3.0: pkt1 arrives intact, but its ack1 is lost. The sender times out and resends pkt1, which also arrives intact. How many times is pkt1's data delivered to the receiving application?
questions.explain: Once. The receiver delivers the first copy, recognizes the retransmission as a duplicate by its sequence number, and only re-sends ack1.

questions.q: In rdt3.0, a premature timeout (one that fires even though nothing was lost) breaks correctness, because the receiver ends up delivering duplicate data.
questions.explain: A premature timeout costs extra transmissions but does not break correctness. Sequence numbers let the receiver discard the duplicate packet, and the sender ignores the resulting extra ACK.

questions.q: rdt3.0: the sender sends pkt0 (ACKed), then pkt1, which is lost. After a timeout it resends pkt1, which is ACKed. What sequence number does the next new data packet carry?
questions.explain: The sequence number alternates only when a new packet is sent. A retransmission keeps the same number. After pkt1 is finally ACKed, the next new packet is pkt0.

questions.q: Which mechanism lets the receiver tell that an arriving packet is a retransmission of data it has already delivered?
choices: Sequence numbers
Checksum
Countdown timer
NAK
questions.explain: Sequence numbers identify retransmitted packets, so duplicates can be discarded instead of delivered up.

questions.q: Which mechanism lets the receiver detect that bits in a packet were flipped?
choices: Checksum
Sequence numbers
Countdown timer
Duplicate ACKs
questions.explain: Error-detection bits such as a checksum reveal changed bits in a packet.

questions.q: Which mechanism lets the sender recover when a packet, or the ACK for it, disappears entirely?
choices: A countdown timer: on timeout, retransmit
A NAK from the receiver
A stronger checksum
A 1-bit sequence number alone
questions.explain: When something is lost, no reply ever arrives, so feedback-based mechanisms can't trigger recovery. The sender's timeout followed by retransmission handles loss (rdt3.0).

questions.q: Which is the first rdt version to use sequence numbers?
choices: rdt1.0
rdt2.0
rdt2.1
rdt3.0
questions.explain: rdt2.1 adds a 1-bit sequence number to fix rdt2.0's problem with garbled ACK/NAKs. rdt2.2 and rdt3.0 keep it.

questions.q: Which of these appear in the rdt3.0 sender's FSM?
choices: A checksum in each packet (make_pkt(..., checksum))
Sequence numbers 0 and 1
A countdown timer (start_timer / stop_timer / timeout)
Retransmission of the current packet
Handling of NAKs from the receiver
questions.explain: rdt3.0 builds on the NAK-free rdt2.2. It uses checksums, alternating 0/1 sequence numbers, ACKs that carry sequence numbers, retransmission, and a timer. It uses no NAKs: it checks isACK(rcvpkt,0) or isACK(rcvpkt,1).
